title: Reading it whole
hookLine: the only prophet's story told complete in one surah
tomorrow: A lesson for those with minds

cards: Musa's story in the Qur'an is everywhere. A scene in al-Baqarah, a long stretch in al-A'raf, his childhood in Ta Ha, his journey with a mysterious teacher in al-Kahf, Pharaoh's last words in Yunus.
You put it together like a puzzle, across the whole book. Many prophets' stories are told that way, each surah taking the piece it needs. Yusuf is different.
One surah, a hundred and eleven verses, beginning, middle and end. It can be read the way a novel is read: whole, in one sitting, so you can see its shape.

teach.h: A DREAM, AND ITS COMING TRUE.
teach.b: Read it whole, and patterns appear that you'd never catch in pieces. Start with the frame. Near the beginning, a boy tells his father a dream: eleven stars, the sun and the moon, bowing to him.

Near the end, his parents and his brothers bow before him, and Yusuf says: this is the meaning of my dream from long ago. The whole surah lives between the telling of one dream and its coming true. Then watch the shirt.

It appears three times. First, the brothers bring it home stained with false blood, to tell their father a wolf ate him. Second, in Egypt, it's torn from behind, and the tear proves Yusuf was running away, not toward.
Third, Yusuf sends it home, and when it's laid on his blind father's face, his sight comes back.

teach.h: A LIE, THE TRUTH, THEN HEALING.
teach.b: A lie, then the truth, then healing, all through the same piece of cloth. Then listen to the father.
When the brothers come home with the bloody shirt, Ya'qub says: sabrun jamil, beautiful patience, the line you carried last year. Years later, when another son is held in Egypt, he says it again.
Twice, in the worst moments. Commentators describe it as patience without complaint to people, while still pouring out grief to God, which Ya'qub does. None of this jumps out from one verse.
A dream that closes, a shirt that changes meaning, a phrase that returns.
You only see the design when you read it whole.

how: Some Muslims read Surah Yusuf straight through, at home or in study circles, and teachers point out its patterns: the dream that opens and closes it, the shirt that appears three times, and Ya'qub's 'beautiful patience.'

o: a handsome reward that waits for the patient
patience with no complaint to people, grief told to God
staying calm by hiding all your sadness, even from God

games.q: the shirt, three times — tap the pairs.

s: the surah opens with a dream and closes with it coming true
this is the meaning of my dream from long ago, Yusuf says near the end.
twice: when the bloody shirt comes, and when another son is held in Egypt.
Musa's story is also told in a single surah
his story is spread across many surahs; Yusuf's is told whole in one.

games.q: your sons come home with a bloody shirt and a story about a wolf. you suspect it isn't true. what does Ya'qub say?
o: I'll never speak to you again.
games.why: sabrun jamil, beautiful patience; and God's help is sought against what you describe. he says it again years later.

practice: If you pray, begin with bismillah. Then picture the three appearances of the shirt, one per breath: false blood, torn from behind, laid on a father's face. Hold the last one longest, the same cloth, now healing.

wordCard.voice: Sabrun jamil. Beautiful patience, the phrase Ya'qub says twice in Surah Yusuf, patience without complaint to people while grief pours out to God. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "beautiful patience," Ya'qub's words in 12:18 and 12:83.

carryVoice: Your line: read it whole. A shape only shows from far enough back. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Qur'an 12:18; 12:83; 12:86 (beautiful patience; grief poured out to God)
